day-1.t: Day 1 — What Django is and your first project

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know what Django does
Install it in a virtual environment
See your first page in the browser

b.v: About 30 minutes. Finish the Python course first – Django is written in Python.

Django is a free Python framework for building websites and APIs. It gives you the parts almost every site needs – URLs, pages, a database, user logins, an admin panel and security – so you write only what is special about your site. Instagram, Pinterest and XpertCreation itself are built with Django.
1) What you need

v: Python 3.10 or newer (python.org) – tick 'Add Python to PATH' on Windows
A code editor – VS Code is free
A terminal – Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on Mac and Linux

b.v: 2) Make a project folder and a virtual environment
A virtual environment keeps each project's packages separate, so one project never breaks another.

@Terminal
mkdir myblog
cd myblog
python -m venv venv

# Windows
venv\Scripts\activate
# Mac / Linux
source venv/bin/activate

pip install django
When the venv is active you see (venv) at the start of the line. Activate it again every time you open a new terminal.
3) Start the project and run it
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser. The rocket page means Django is working. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
4) What was created

v: manage.py = the command tool you use for everything
config/settings.py = all settings: apps, database, time zone, security
config/urls.py = the list of web addresses your site answers
db.sqlite3 = a small database file, created when you first run the project

b.v: Never put your real SECRET_KEY or passwords in code you share on GitHub. You will learn the safe way on Day 10.
Today's goal

v: Create an app
Write a view
Connect a URL to it

b.v: About 30 minutes.
A Django project is made of apps. Each app does one job – blog, accounts, shop. Today you create the blog app.

@Terminal
python manage.py startapp blog
Tell Django about it: open config/settings.py and add 'blog' to INSTALLED_APPS.

@Python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.admin",
    "django.contrib.auth",
    "django.contrib.contenttypes",
    "django.contrib.sessions",
    "django.contrib.messages",
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "blog",
]
1) A view is a function that returns a page
2) Connect the URLs

@Python
# blog/urls.py  (make this new file)
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.home, name="home"),
    path("about/", views.about, name="about"),
]

@Python
# config/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("", include("blog.urls")),
]
Run the server and open / and /about/. Each address runs its view.
3) A URL with a value in it
Open /hello/Ayesha/. The part in the address arrives in the view as name.
Today's goal

v: Return real HTML pages
Show values with {{ }}
Use one base layout for every page

b.v: About 30 minutes.
Writing HTML inside Python strings gets messy fast. Templates are HTML files with small placeholders that Django fills in.
1) Your first template
Make the folders blog/templates/blog/ and create home.html inside.

v: {{ name }} = print a value (Django escapes it, so it is safe from HTML injection)
{% for %} ... {% endfor %} = repeat for each item
{% if %} ... {% else %} ... {% endif %} = show something only sometimes
{{ text|upper }} = a filter changes how a value looks (upper, length, date, truncatewords)

b.v: 2) One layout for all pages

@HTML {% block title %}My Blog{% endblock %}
Home | About
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
{% url 'home' %} builds the link from the name you gave in urls.py. If you change the address later, every link still works.
Today's goal

v: Describe your data as a model
Create the table with migrations
Know the common field types

b.v: About 30 minutes.
A model is a Python class that describes one kind of thing you store – a post, a product, a task. Django turns it into a database table for you. You don't write SQL.

@Python
# blog/models.py
from django.db import models
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    body = models.TextField()
    author = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title
1) Create the table

v: makemigrations = Django writes a plan of the change (a migration file)
migrate = Django applies the plan to the database
Run both every time you change a model

b.v: 2) Common fields

v: CharField = short text, needs max_length
TextField = long text
IntegerField / DecimalField = numbers (use DecimalField for money)
BooleanField = yes / no
DateField / DateTimeField = dates and times
ForeignKey = a link to another model (many posts belong to one author)
ImageField / FileField = uploads (ImageField needs the Pillow package)

b.v: Never delete migration files by hand once you have shared or deployed them. Make a new migration instead.
Today's goal

v: Create an admin user
Manage posts without writing any pages
Make the admin list useful

b.v: About 20 minutes.
Django gives you a full admin panel for free. Many companies run their whole back office on it.

@Terminal
python manage.py createsuperuser
Open /admin/, sign in, and add three posts. Try the search box and the filters on the right.

v: list_display = which columns the list shows
list_filter = filters in the side bar
search_fields = which fields the search box looks in

b.v: Use the admin for your team, not for your visitors. Visitors get the pages you build yourself.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Reading and saving data (the ORM)

b.v: Today's goal

v: Fetch, filter and sort records
Create, update and delete in Python
Show posts on the home page

b.v: About 30 minutes.
The ORM lets you talk to the database in Python. Try it in the Django shell.

@Terminal
python manage.py shell

@Python
from blog.models import Post
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

Post.objects.all()                                  # every post
Post.objects.filter(published=True)                 # only published
Post.objects.filter(title__icontains="django")      # title contains 'django'
Post.objects.order_by("-created")[:5]               # newest five
Post.objects.count()

p = Post.objects.get(id=1)                          # exactly one (error if missing)
p.title = "A better title"
p.save()                                            # update

me = User.objects.first()
Post.objects.create(title="New", body="Hi", author=me)   # insert
Post.objects.filter(published=False).delete()            # delete
1) Show the posts on the home page
get_object_or_404 shows a proper 'not found' page instead of crashing when the post does not exist.
Today's goal

v: Build a form from a model
Handle GET and POST
Validate input safely

b.v: About 30 minutes.

v: GET = show the empty form
POST = the user pressed Save; check it and save it
form.is_valid() = runs every check; if it fails, the same page shows the errors
redirect after saving = stops a refresh from saving the post twice

b.v: Always keep {% csrf_token %} inside POST forms. It stops other websites from submitting forms in your users' name.
Today's goal

v: Add sign in and sign out
Protect pages with login_required
Let people edit only their own posts

b.v: About 30 minutes.

@Python
# config/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("accounts/", include("django.contrib.auth.urls")),   # login, logout, password reset
    path("", include("blog.urls")),
]

# config/settings.py
LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = "home"
LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = "home"
1) Only signed-in users can write
Hiding a button is not security. Always check ownership in the view, like post_edit does above.
In Django 5 and newer, sign out must be a POST form, as shown. A plain link to /accounts/logout/ no longer works.

day-9.t: Day 9 — A JSON API with Django REST Framework

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know what an API is
Turn your posts into JSON
Get ready to connect a React front end

b.v: About 35 minutes. This lesson is the bridge to the React course and the live project.

So far Django has made the HTML. In modern apps, Django often only sends data (JSON), and a separate front end – a React website or a mobile app – draws the screen. The part that sends data is called an API.

@Terminal
pip install djangorestframework
Add 'rest_framework' to INSTALLED_APPS.

@Python
# blog/api.py
from rest_framework import generics
from .models import Post
from .serializers import PostSerializer

class PostList(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = Post.objects.filter(published=True).order_by("-created")
    serializer_class = PostSerializer

class PostDetail(generics.RetrieveAPIView):
    queryset = Post.objects.filter(published=True)
    serializer_class = PostSerializer

@Python
# blog/urls.py
from . import api
urlpatterns += [
    path("api/posts/", api.PostList.as_view()),
    path("api/posts/<int:pk>/", api.PostDetail.as_view()),
]
Open /api/posts/. You see your posts as JSON, in a page DRF draws so you can explore it.

v: Serializer = turns model objects into JSON and checks incoming JSON
Generic views = ready-made API views for list, detail, create, update, delete
ViewSets and routers = even shorter; you will use them in the live project

day-10.t: Day 10 — Going live safely, and your mini blog

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know the settings that must change before going live
Know how Django runs on a real server
Check your finished mini blog

b.v: About 30 minutes.
1) Settings for production

@Python
# config/settings.py
import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]          # never in code
DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG") == "1"         # off in production
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["myblog.example.com"]
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ["https://myblog.example.com"]
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "staticfiles"
DEBUG = True on a live site shows your code and settings to anyone who causes an error. Always switch it off.
2) How it runs on a server

v: Gunicorn = runs your Django app (python manage.py runserver is only for your own computer)
Nginx = the web server in front: handles HTTPS and serves static files
PostgreSQL = the usual database for live sites (SQLite is fine for learning)
collectstatic = copies CSS, JS and images into STATIC_ROOT for Nginx

b.v:
@Terminal
pip install gunicorn
python manage.py collectstatic
python manage.py check --deploy
gunicorn config.wsgi --bind 127.0.0.1:8000
python manage.py check --deploy lists the security settings you still need to fix. Run it before every launch.
3) Your mini blog – checklist

You should now have all of this working.|A home page listing published posts, newest first|A page for each post|Sign in and sign out|A 'Write' page that only signed-in users can open|Editing allowed only for the author|The admin with search and filters|A JSON API at /api/posts/
